item.title: Contractor to Civil Servant: NASA Welcomes Jared Spiers
item.description: Jared Spiers had an interest in contributing to NASA’s mission long before becoming a civil servant for the agency. Growing up close to NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, and hearing about his father’s work there, he gained a firsthand connection to the nation’s space program. Before graduating high school, he knew […]

item.title: A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms
item.description: Scientists have identified a weakened brain signal that may connect several seemingly unrelated symptoms of schizophrenia, including sensory processing difficulties, disorganized speech, and greater symptom severity. The surprising discovery could help explain the disorder's underlying mechanisms and potentially lead to earlier detection and new treatments.

item.title: Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
item.description: A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, raising concerns about the long-term brain health effects of common sugar substitutes, although causation was not established.

item.title: A 700,000-year-old elephant tooth reveals a lost world where early humans lived
item.description: A remarkably preserved elephant tooth dating back nearly 700,000 years has revealed a surprisingly lush prehistoric world where giant elephants and early humans lived side by side. Discovered in northern Israel alongside ancient stone tools, the tooth belonged to a straight-tusked elephant, one of the largest land mammals of the Ice Age.

item.title: NASA discovers Jupiter’s invisible shield is more complex than Earth’s
item.description: NASA’s Juno spacecraft has discovered that Jupiter uses a surprisingly complex system of powerful plasma waves and multiple shock regions to defend against the solar wind. The findings reveal major differences between Jupiter and Earth and could help scientists understand the enormous shock waves produced by exploding stars.

item.title: Einstein's equations may explain the universe without dark energy
item.description: Mathematicians have uncovered what they argue is a fundamental flaw in the standard model of the universe, potentially challenging the need for dark energy. Their calculations suggest that the mathematical framework used to describe cosmic expansion is inherently unstable and that the universe could accelerate naturally under Einstein's original theory of gravity. The findings also raise surprising questions about whether our location in the universe is as ordinary as scientists have long assumed.

item.title: Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk
item.description: Getting more daylight could be linked to a surprisingly powerful benefit for brain health. In a study of more than 87,000 adults, researchers found that higher daytime light exposure was associated with a 16% lower risk of dementia, with longer exposure to bright light linked to even greater reductions. Remarkably, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors.

item.title: Scientists discover that cranberry juice may help fight tooth decay
item.description: Cranberry juice may offer an unexpected benefit beyond its reputation for helping prevent urinary tract infections: protecting teeth from decay. Researchers at the University of Illinois Chicago discovered that pure, unsweetened cranberry juice slowed the regrowth of dental plaque bacteria and reduced their production of acids that damage tooth enamel. The secret may lie in naturally occurring compounds called proanthocyanidins, which interfere with harmful bacteria.

item.title: 128,000-year-old ice in Tibet could rewrite climate history
item.description: Ancient ice discovered high in Tibet may be more than 128,000 years old, preserving an extraordinary record of Earth's climate that scientists previously thought had been lost. The discovery reveals a rare glimpse into the last ice age and could reshape our understanding of how glaciers survive dramatic changes in global climate.

item.title: Arnab Strikes India
item.description: The first named storm of the North Indian Ocean’s cyclone season made landfall along the coast of Andhra Pradesh.

item.title: Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal
item.description: Researchers have discovered a small group of brain cells that prevents dangerous blood pressure swings, even when average readings appear normal. The finding reveals a hidden source of cardiovascular risk and could open the door to new treatments that protect the heart and brain.

item.title: Scientists just broke a textbook rule of physics
item.description: Scientists have defied a long-standing rule of laser physics by generating X-rays with much higher energies than conventional theory predicts. The surprising discovery reveals how two electrons working together can overcome a previously accepted limit, opening new possibilities for quantum research.

item.title: Meteors don't just burn up. What really happens is far more violent
item.description: Scientists have uncovered seven surprising stages that space rocks go through as they hurtle toward Earth, revealing that melting and violent fragmentation, rather than simple evaporation, determine their fate. The discovery could help explain why meteorites scatter across the ground and how dangerous asteroids explode in Earth's atmosphere.

item.title: Caltech Names Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman as NASA JPL Deputy
item.description: Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman has been named Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The emeritus astronaut and retired U.S. Navy captain begins his new role at NASA’s center of excellence for robotics and deep space exploration and at Caltech, which manages JPL for NASA, on […]

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden oxygen reservoir deep inside Earth
item.description: Scientists have discovered that magma deep inside Earth can store surprising amounts of extra oxygen, potentially revealing a hidden contributor to our planet's oxygen-rich atmosphere. The findings suggest that ancient volcanic eruptions may have helped transform Earth's atmosphere billions of years ago, with implications for understanding life on other planets.

item.title: Even stupendous black holes can’t explain dark matter
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03386-4 The theoretical objects would have left a larger imprint on cosmic radiation if they were a source of the invisible force pulling together the galaxies.

item.title: NASA Welcomes Vietnam as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory
item.description: The Socialist Republic of Vietnam became the 78th nation to sign the Artemis Accords, joining a growing coalition of like-minded nations committed to the peaceful, transparent, and responsible exploration of space. “Vietnam is joining at an important point in the development of its own space program,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson in recorded remarks […]

item.title: Artemis III SLS Core Stage Joins Boosters at Kennedy
item.description: NASA’s Artemis III SLS (Space Launch System) core stage is integrated alongside the twin solid rocket boosters on Oct. 28 inside the Vehicle Assembly Building’s High Bay 3 at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Technicians lifted the 212-foot rocket stage from the facility’s High Bay 2 using a one-of-a kind lifting beam designed […]

item.title: NASA University Challenge Ignites Trajectory of Drone Entrepreneur
item.description: Five years ago, Gavin Gardner was a Michigan State University engineering student researching next-generation drone technology as part of a NASA grant. Garder expected the research to be demanding – but he was surprised that navigating the financial side of the work presented an even greater challenge. Although Gardner was used to leading fellow students […]

item.title: NASA Selects 19 New Citizen Science Proposals in 2026
item.description: So far, 2026 has seen a flood of successes for volunteers who do NASA science, exemplifying NASA’s commitment to gold-standard science—transparent, reproducible and intrinsically collaborative. The Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 project announced that their project volunteers have now discovered most of the known brown dwarfs, celestial objects that are similar to planets. The Zooniverse platform, […]

item.title: Webb Sees Turbulent Star Nursery
item.description: In this Webb image released on Oct. 22, 2026, we see a turbulent cauldron of star formation filled with dense clumps of gas. This region is named N159 and is located 161,000 light-years away in the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the satellite galaxies orbiting the Milky Way galaxy. This region has a lower metallicity […]

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden reason why muscles weaken with age
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a hidden defense mechanism in aging muscles that sacrifices strength to protect cells from damage. In mice, partially restoring a crucial molecule reversed signs of muscle wasting and prevented premature death, raising hopes for new treatments for age-related muscle decline.

item.title: A single sauna session sends immune cells surging through your body
item.description: A new Finnish study reveals that just 30 minutes in a sauna can temporarily flood the bloodstream with additional white blood cells, potentially helping the immune system patrol the body and detect threats. The surprising response resembles the immune boost seen during exercise and may help explain some of the health benefits linked to sauna bathing.

item.title: Smaller EV batteries, longer range? Scientists may have found a way
item.description: Scientists have developed a new technology that could make electric vehicle batteries smaller, lighter, and longer-lasting, potentially allowing cars to travel farther on a single charge. By borrowing precision manufacturing techniques from computer chip production, they found a way to prevent damaging lithium buildup that has held back next-generation batteries.

item.title: Scientists discover a secret glow in toxic fire salamanders
item.description: Researchers have discovered a surprising hidden ability in Europe's familiar black-and-yellow fire salamanders: they glow green and cyan under ultraviolet light. The mysterious fluorescence comes mainly from glands in their skin and their toxic secretions, which can continue glowing for more than 24 hours after being released.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden 100-million-year-old volcanic system
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a long-lost volcanic system in Iran that dates back roughly 100 million years, revealing a hidden chapter in Earth's tectonic history. The discovery sheds new light on the disappearance of an ancient ocean and the powerful geological forces that reshaped the Middle East.

item.title: Earth's ice ages may have been driven by a hidden ocean chain reaction
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising connection between Earth's opposite poles that may help explain how the planet plunged into past ice ages. New research suggests that as massive ice sheets expanded across the Northern Hemisphere, they cooled Atlantic Ocean waters that eventually traveled south toward Antarctica. This cooling may have disrupted Southern Ocean circulation, allowing the ocean to absorb and store more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, further cooling the planet.

item.title: NASA’s Artemis I mission reveals surprising radiation levels near the Moon
item.description: NASA’s Artemis I mission has revealed that cosmic radiation near the Moon is higher than in Earth orbit, but not by as much as scientists might expect. Tiny experimental detectors also uncovered surprising details about how radiation passes through the human body, offering valuable insights for future lunar exploration.

item.title: Antarctica’s “Doomsday Glacier” could raise sea levels twice as much as predicted
item.description: Antarctica’s Thwaites Glacier may be melting twice as much as previously predicted, even without additional global warming. Scientists discovered that warm ocean water is penetrating miles beneath the ice, weakening its foundations and accelerating its retreat. A new model predicts that the glacier could add up to 30 millimeters to global sea levels by 2100, with a 60% chance of losing a crucial stabilizing ridge.

item.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5043-5049: Preparing to Drill at ‘Nazca’
item.description: Written by Lucy Lim, Planetary Scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center Earth planning date: Friday, Oct. 16, 2026 Following the Basque Lakes drill campaign, Curiosity has returned to a spot just a few meters away from the “Chiu Chiu” block to conduct our next drill campaign. “Chiu Chiu” itself wasn’t a good candidate for […]

item.title: A simple daily fiber supplement reduced arthritis pain and improved strength
item.description: A new clinical trial suggests that a simple daily fiber supplement could significantly reduce knee osteoarthritis pain, improve muscle strength, and make the body less sensitive to pain. Researchers discovered that the benefits may be linked to changes in gut bacteria and the hormone GLP-1, revealing a promising new approach to arthritis relief.

item.title: The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
item.description: A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children. The discovery could help explain why some autistic people have difficulty recognizing faces and reading emotions.

item.title: The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have helped ants conquer the world
item.description: The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have set the stage for ants to conquer the planet, with a surprising boost from “jumping genes” hidden in their DNA. Scientists discovered that bursts of activity from these mobile genetic elements coincided with the rise of major ant groups and may have helped sharpen their extraordinary ability to communicate through smell.

item.title: Scientists discover the immune system’s hidden sense of touch
item.description: Scientists at McGill University have discovered a surprising new ability of immune cells that could change how we understand long-term immunity. Researchers found that T cells can actually sense how stiff their surrounding tissues are, using these physical signals to help determine whether they develop into long-lasting memory cells that protect against future infections.

item.title: Switchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions

item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11335-4 Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination

item.title: Why did ancient humans avoid this lush paradise
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03486-1 A new expedition into the Rub’ al Khali desert finds no evidence of ancient human settlement.

item.title: This Arabian desert was once a lush paradise. Why did ancient humans avoid it?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03484-3 Expedition revealed that water wasn’t enough for human settlement — plus, proposals to block sunlight get serious.

item.title: Accounting of Africa’s water reveals a management gap
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03260-3 A map of Africa’s water demand reveals that the scarcity of water is only part of the problem facing the continent — management is a separate challenge.

item.title: The brain liquidates billions of mutant neurons around the time we’re born
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03444-x Faulty neurons can contribute to various neurological conditions, but researchers have uncovered a system that might clean them up.

item.title: Daily briefing: The big push to personalize psychiatry
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03531-z A data-driven approach could match treatments to individuals with more precision. Plus, funders in Europe are backing preprint-led publishing and whether professors should care about student evaluations.

item.title: Tethered to stone: how rock and water availability shaped early desert occupation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03263-0 Fresh water in deserts often points to sites with signs of early humans and stone tools. But, in Arabia’s Rub’ al Khali region, water alone does not predict occupation.

item.title: What students think about my teaching doesn’t matter. Am I wrong?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02202-3 A jury weighs in on whether teaching assessments are popularity contests or an important tool.

item.title: How personalization and psychedelics are revitalizing psychiatry
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03402-7 Fresh ideas are welcome in a discipline in which progress is rare — provided they are applied rigorously.

item.title: Lactate takes a shortcut into mitochondria to power the heart
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03261-2 A cellular fuel called lactate is channelled directly into energy-generating organelles in heart muscle, defying the prevailing view about lactate transport.

item.title: Clues about complex life come from freshly cultivated archaea
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03294-7 Two archaeal strains that belong to a lineage closely related to the ancestor of eukaryotic cells (complex cells with membrane-bound organelles) have been brought into culture. Their simple internal organization, elaborate surface structures, microbial partnerships and protein-dependent lifestyle provide clues about how eukaryotic cells arose.

item.title: Preprint-centric publishing model gets major boost
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03445-w European funders put weight behind emerging ‘publish, review, curate’ approach for preprints.

item.title: These three red flags could unmask dodgy journals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03325-3 As poor publishing practices proliferate, scholarly databases are under pressure to ensure the titles they list are reputable.

item.title: Is research funding now a lottery? Elite funder ERC swamped by applications
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03476-3 A marked rise in submissions for the European Research Council’s grants is pushing down success rates.

item.title: Dengue comes back even in vaccinated people — new clues
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03488-z Researchers help to answer a question dogging the development of improved vaccines against the mosquito-borne disease.

item.title: The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03391-7 Could a blood sample, a brain scan and a look at your phone data transform how your psychiatrist treats you?

item.title: Could a giant sunshade in space ‘solve global warming’? Scientists are taking the idea seriously
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03415-2 Some say the concept is complete fantasy, but a detailed analysis suggests that the falling cost of rocket launches might make it feasible in a few decades.

item.title: An unexpected function of a cell-cycle enzyme might explain the toxic effects of its inhibitors
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03288-5 A previously unknown mechanism required for cells to start proliferating has been identified. A combination of mathematical modelling and cell-based experiments shows that the enzyme WEE1 switches off a protein-degradation complex to allow cell proliferation to start, with implications for WEE1 inhibitors currently in trials for cancer treatments.

item.title: Meta-study sparks questions about what it means to be good at regulating emotions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03262-1 A first-of-its kind consortium reveals a lack of correlation between behavioural and neural measures of a person’s emotional regulation.

item.title: How the pandemic changed trust in science — in four charts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03248-z The largest analysis of its kind reveals the public’s changing relationship with science and the people who do it.

item.title: Genetic variants that alter gene regulation in specific cell types are closely tied to disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03067-2 Single-cell profiling of nearly 2,000 people brings scientists closer to understanding the link between genetic variation, gene expression and health.

item.title: Ribbon made of carbon pentagons and heptagons has metallic properties
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03298-3 Ribbons that are composed exclusively of five- and seven-carbon rings have metal-like electron transport and conductance. The ribbons can be synthesized by linking previously inaccessible chains of paired five-membered rings, providing a route to making highly conducting carbon nanoribbons.

item.title: Where have all the saucers flown?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03107-x Missed encounters.

item.title: The shifting sands of research independence: why mid-career scientists crave security
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02670-7 A project to improve understanding of an often-neglected group in academia aims to help its members to navigate career uncertainty.

item.title: Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11180-5 A geoarchaeological survey of the Rub’ al Khali (the Empty Quarter of Arabia) and spatial modelling of the Arabian Peninsula suggest that human settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and stone suitable for making tools, rather than water alone.

item.title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11211-1 A subset of necrotizing enterocolitis in infants is mediated specifically by the Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin.

item.title: Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10438-2 Whole-genome sequencing and cell-level gene expression measurements show that length variation in tandem repeats in the human genome contributes to cell type-specific differences in gene regulation and expression, as well as the architecture of complex traits.

item.title: Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11223-x Pseudo-direct bandgap character in bismuth sulfide retards bimolecular electron–hole recombination while preserving strong light absorption.

item.title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11190-3 Single-neuron sequencing shows that widespread genomic abnormalities are common prenatally but largely eliminated around birth, indicating developmental genome quality control in human neurons.

item.title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11195-y Computational simulations of a neural network based on fly connectomes identify a three-neuron circuit that is organized to produce leg motor rhythms for walking.

item.title: Narrow carbon pentaheptite nanoribbon as a covalent metal
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11202-2 Planar carbon pentaheptite nanoribbons are synthesized by laterally fusing polypentalene chains transformed from pre-synthesized polycyclooctadiene chains, suggesting a possible route towards carbon quantum wires.

item.title: Molecular underpinnings of rheumatic diseases and emerging therapeutic concepts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10966-x Improved molecular insights into inflammatory rheumatic diseases are enabling better disease control and advancing the field towards achieving durable remission and eventual cure.

item.title: Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11214-y An experimental concept enabling attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone is demonstrated and used to visualize the lightwave-driven electron motion of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene.

item.title: Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11181-4 Dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory.

item.title: T and B cells recognize splicing-derived neutrophil neoantigens in lupus
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11219-7 In systemic lupus erythematosus, aberrant splicing in neutrophils generates novel peptides that are presented on MHC I, driving CD4+ and CD8+ T cell activation, clonal expansion and IgG autoantibody responses, establishing neoantigen-driven autoimmune immunity.

item.title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10721-2 Phase 1 of TenK10K takes single-cell RNA sequencing and matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals, enabling detection of associations for common and rare genetic variants, the latter of which have been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression.

item.title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11203-1 Sensorimotor and amygdala activation, but not canonical prefrontal control circuits, indicate emotion regulation capacity.

item.title: Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour–CAF–T cell crosstalk in renal cancer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11208-w Tumour assembloids, which model components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts and tumour-infiltrating immune cells, are used to identify an essential pathway that mediates heterogeneous therapeutic responses.

item.title: MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11182-3 In mouse myocardium, glucose oxidation persists in the absence of the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, with mitochondrial MCT1 importing lactate into mitochondria and LDHB oxidizing it to pyruvate and NADH, sustaining cardiac energetics and preventing stress-induced heart failure.

item.title: Eukaryotes’ closest relatives are internally simple syntrophic peptidotrophic archaea
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11170-7 Cultures reveal conservation of cell structure, physical symbioses and anaerobiosis across Heimdallarchaeia (the archaeal lineage that branches closest to eukaryotes) and other Promethearchaeota.

item.title: Monolithically and in situ integrated PbS infrared imagers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11222-y A method for growing infrared image sensors directly from solution using raw materials by monolithic in situ integration of high-performance semiconductor PbS photodetectors on readout integrated circuits is described, yielding films with excellent electronic properties.

item.title: Time-reversal-symmetry-breaking spin injection from a compensated magnet
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11227-7 Experiments show that altermagnetic Mn5Si3 generates spin currents despite zero net magnetization, demonstrating a central prediction of altermagnetic spintronics.

item.title: A single-molecule spin–photon interface
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11147-6 A triplet carbene molecule in a tailored crystal provides a stable single-molecule spin–photon interface with millisecond coherence, advancing chemically engineered molecular qubits for quantum networking.

item.title: Presynaptic homeostasis mediated by exocytosis of a SNARE protein
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11201-3 Experiments show that when subjected to high-frequency stimulation, excitatory neurons exhibit a presynaptic form of homeostatic plasticity mediated by the exocytosis of v-SNARE protein VAMP7 and the resulting inhibition of P/Q-type calcium channels.

item.title: Spatial and sectoral water demand assessment for the African continent
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11199-8 Africa-wide water demand analysis across six sectors in 2020 shows that in specific regions of northern and southern Africa, the current water demand exceeds water availability.

item.title: Alzheimer’s disease genetics converges on microglial and neuronal dysregulation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11206-y A multi-ancestry study of Alzheimer’s disease identifies new risk loci and potential drug targets, implicates microglia and neurons, and reveals a larger common-variant contribution than previously estimated.

item.title: Genetic variants shape single-cell chromatin accessibility and disease risk
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11173-4 Single-cell chromatin accessibility profiling identifies cell-type-specific and cell-state-specific genetic effects that link non-coding variants to immune disease risk.

item.title: Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11178-z Pharmacological inhibition of the m7G methyltransferase METTL1 in vivo impairs tumour growth and substantially prolongs survival in multiple mouse cancer models of different tissue origin.

item.title: SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11197-w Loss of function of canonical BAF induces gain of CTCF and cohesin binding that alters 3D genome architecture and reprograms transcription.

item.title: The secret to slower aging may be hiding in your gut
item.description: The secret to aging more slowly may be hiding in your gut. Scientists discovered that certain gut bacteria are strongly linked to how quickly the body ages, with microbial differences accounting for about 15% of the variation in biological aging rates. Some bacterial species were associated with slower aging, while others were linked to accelerated aging.

item.title: Low testosterone may make sugar far more harmful to your liver
item.description: Scientists have discovered that low testosterone and a high-fructose diet can work together to worsen fatty liver disease in mice. Unexpectedly, changes in gut bacteria appear to drive this harmful interaction, revealing a potential new target for preventing liver damage.

item.title: Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body
item.description: A surprising discovery reveals that widely used anti-inflammatory drugs may unintentionally help dangerous viruses spread through the body. Scientists found that JAK inhibitors, prescribed for rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases, can weaken a crucial immune defense against influenza, COVID-19, and other infections. By suppressing genes that normally fight viruses, these medications may leave patients more vulnerable to infection.

item.title: James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”
item.description: A scorching lava planet 280 light-years away has surprised astronomers by apparently maintaining a thick atmosphere despite conditions that should have stripped it away billions of years ago. James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest that TOI-561 b reflects about 75% of incoming starlight, possibly because of mineral clouds that act like a giant sunscreen. The planet may also be continually replenishing its atmosphere through gases released from a global ocean of molten rock.

item.title: Smithsonian scientists just recreated the first 2 billion years of the Universe
item.description: Scientists have created one of the largest and most detailed simulations of the early universe ever made, offering an extraordinary new glimpse into the cosmos shortly after the Big Bang. Called Lumina, the groundbreaking simulation recreates the universe’s first 2 billion years, showing how dark matter, gas, and radiation interacted to give rise to the earliest stars, galaxies, and black holes.

item.title: A tiny laser beam could make computer memory 1,000 times faster
item.description: Scientists at UC San Diego have developed a surprising new way to store digital information using light instead of magnets, potentially paving the way for smaller, faster, and more energy-efficient memory devices. By precisely shaping and shrinking an ultrafast laser beam, researchers demonstrated that they could switch magnetic states in a material, the basic process used to write digital data. The technique could potentially operate more than 1,000 times faster than conventional magnetic switching methods.

item.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
item.description: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s
item.description: Why do some people stay mentally sharp even when their brains show signs of Alzheimer’s disease? Scientists in the Netherlands may have uncovered an important clue hidden in a rare group of immature brain cells. Researchers discovered that these cells remain present even in people over 80, but their behavior differs dramatically between those who develop dementia and those who remain cognitively healthy.

item.title: Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging
item.description: Mayo Clinic scientists have uncovered surprising new insights into “zombie cells,” aging cells that linger in the body and contribute to inflammation and disease. Seven studies reveal why these cells are harmful and identify new strategies for targeting them, including a natural compound found in tomatoes. In aging mice, experimental treatments reduced inflammation and improved physical and brain health. The findings could open the door to therapies that combat some of the biological processes behind aging.

item.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
item.description: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

item.title: The surprisingly simple exercise that could lower your blood pressure
item.description: A surprisingly simple exercise routine could help lower blood pressure without requiring daily workouts or expensive equipment. In a study of 100 adults, researchers found that wall squats performed just once or twice a week helped maintain significant reductions in systolic blood pressure over the short term.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03385-5 Genomic analysis shows that the owls spread from Eurasia to the Caribbean, then colonized the rest of the Western Hemisphere.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02814-9 Misplaced or borrowed laboratory equipment can bring experiments to a halt. Scientists explain how they stop essential kit from going missing.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03482-5 Despite setbacks, pharma companies are betting big on psychedelic drugs to treat mental-health conditions. Plus, longevity researchers are turning their attention to pets and how to keep tabs on the tools in your lab.

item.title: Why pharma firms are betting billions on psychedelic drugs despite setbacks
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03390-8 Regulatory pushback stalled the field. But researchers are optimistic about mind-altering drugs as potential treatments for depression and mood disorders.

item.title: Revered NASA spacecraft is about to perish in flames — astronomers are mourning
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03461-w A failed rescue mission means that the Swift observatory will fall into Earth’s atmosphere next week, but it leaves a massive archive of data for scientists to explore.

item.title: Could measuring immune health reshape medical care?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03396-2 Finding practical ways to analyse the state of a person’s immune system could guide treatment decisions and create opportunities for disease prevention.

item.title: Mysterious flickering brain signals could help to unlock secrets of consciousness
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03384-6 Monkeys’ brain activity flips 15 times per second between patterns linked to objects of which the monkeys are aware and patterns for objects outside their awareness.

item.title: Global climate body fights for survival: why the IPCC must be saved
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03403-6 The UN organization faces perhaps the most serious crisis in its nearly 40-year history — but it is too precious to lose.

item.title: Can scientists reliably tell if a novel is written using AI?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03394-4 Computer scientist Tuhin Chakrabarty talks about detecting AI-generated prose — and why it matters.

item.title: Scientists solve a 30-year mystery behind inflammatory bowel disease
item.description: Scientists have identified a hidden cause of inflammatory bowel disease: antibodies that disable the immune system’s natural ability to control inflammation, potentially explaining severe illness in thousands of patients. The breakthrough also solves a 30-year genetic mystery and could pave the way for more precise diagnoses and targeted treatments.

item.title: Exercise doesn't just strengthen your heart. It rewires it
item.description: Regular exercise does more than strengthen the heart. New research reveals that it actually reshapes the nerves controlling how the heart functions, and the changes are surprisingly different on the left and right sides of the body.

item.title: A 2,700-year-old solar eclipse just revealed something surprising about Earth
item.description: A solar eclipse recorded more than 2,700 years ago is revealing surprising secrets about Earth's rotation and the Sun's ancient behavior. By correcting an eight-kilometer error in the location of an ancient Chinese capital, scientists were able to reconstruct a total solar eclipse that occurred in 709 BCE and obtain more accurate measurements of how fast Earth was spinning at the time.

item.title: Chinese scientists discover “D-rex,” a giant fungus with roots stretching back 65 million years
item.description: Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind. Dubbed “D-rex,” its evolutionary lineage appears to have emerged shortly after the dinosaurs went extinct, raising intriguing questions about how that ancient catastrophe may have shaped its evolution.

item.title: New 3D thermal invisibility cloak makes objects disappear from infrared cameras
item.description: Researchers have developed a groundbreaking 3D invisibility cloak that can hide complex objects from infrared cameras while protecting them from extreme heat and cold. Instead of blocking heat, the device guides it around an object, making the object appear invisible to thermal imaging from virtually any direction. Successfully built and tested, the cloak could transform electronics cooling, thermal protection, and stealth technology.

item.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
item.description: Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.

item.title: Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck
item.description: A mysterious shipwreck off Turkey’s coast may be the oldest ever discovered, dating back approximately 4,500 years to the age of the Egyptian pyramids. Although the wooden vessel has disappeared, its surviving pottery cargo reveals clues about an ancient trading network that may have connected distant Mediterranean civilizations. Researchers believe the ship may have crashed against rocks during a storm while transporting valuable goods such as oil, wine, or tree resin.

item.title: AI detects “invisible” signs of pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis
item.description: A powerful new AI system could help doctors detect pancreatic cancer years before it becomes visible on conventional scans. The technology, called REDMOD, identified hidden warning signs an average of 475 days before diagnosis and was nearly twice as sensitive as experienced radiologists. By spotting cancer-related changes at their earliest stages, it could dramatically improve the chances of successful treatment for one of the deadliest forms of cancer.

item.title: A simple liquid can stop cavities without drilling, major study confirms
item.description: A simple liquid painted onto teeth in seconds can stop cavities without drilling, injections, or anesthesia, according to a major clinical trial involving young children. The inexpensive treatment could spare thousands of children painful dental procedures and surgery while paving the way for broader FDA-approved use.

item.title: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
item.description: Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors.

item.title: Nerve activity initiates autoimmune hair loss
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03258-x Understanding the triggers of autoimmunity might lead to better therapies, with hair loss among the conditions for which underpinning factors have come to light.

item.title: Women might have invented language — but not alone
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03392-6 An eloquent analysis of the origins of human speech suggests that social cohesion, not conflict, drove our use of words.

item.title: Daily briefing: The Selfish Gene, 50 years on
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03463-8 What biologists think of Dawkins’s big idea now. Plus. how the subject of a new film haunts science and a bacterium that makes its own MOFs.

item.title: Are salaries getting worse? Many scientists think so
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03398-0 Nature’s survey of almost 4,000 researchers shows that you’re not alone if you struggle to make ends meet or your last pay rise is a distant memory.

item.title: Can science make your dog live longer? Longevity craze comes to pets
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03447-8 The emerging science — and industry — of animal longevity is attracting interest from companies and academics alike.

item.title: Glimpsing archaeal microbes on the move
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03259-w How and when did cells gain the ability to crawl? Live imaging of cells from close relatives of early eukaryotes fills in a major gap in the understanding of cellular evolution.

item.title: Evolutionary ‘game-changer’: weird armoured amphibian lived in ancient seas
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03440-1 The creature’s armour cladding probably enabled it to tolerate the salty seas of the Late Triassic.

item.title: Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication
item.description: Missing blood pressure medication could mean losing much of its protection against heart attacks and strokes, according to an analysis of more than 91,000 people. Patients who consistently took their medication experienced an 11% reduction in major cardiovascular events, while those who missed too many doses saw little or no measurable benefit.

item.title: Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think
item.description: A major new study reveals that drinking just two alcoholic beverages a day is associated with a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of death from alcohol-related causes, challenging the idea that moderate drinking is harmless. Researchers also found no significant overall health benefits from alcohol, with risks rising as consumption increases.

item.title: Three giant black holes discovered in a galaxy from the dawn of time
item.description: Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding black holes inside a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years away, revealing a remarkable scene from the universe’s infancy. Two of the black holes are separated by just 620 light-years and are expected to eventually merge, while a third lurks farther away. One weighs an astonishing 80 million suns, and another is growing faster than conventional theories predict.

item.title: New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
item.description: Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water. Using machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements, Yale scientists have uncovered surprising clues about which prehistoric creatures truly became aquatic. Their findings suggest that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient marine reptiles previously thought to be fully aquatic actually spent considerable time on land.

item.title: Scientists discover how pancreatic cancer rewrites its DNA to escape treatment
item.description: Scientists have discovered how pancreatic cancer cells continually reshape their genetic makeup to become more aggressive, spread, and evade treatment. In laboratory experiments, blocking a key gene reversed some of these dangerous changes, revealing a potential new way to fight the deadly disease.

item.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
item.description: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not.

item.title: This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans
item.description: For nearly a century, people in distant parts of the world have reported a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or even hundreds of tiny, colorful humans moving through the real world. Now, scientists have identified a mushroom species, Lanmaoa asiatica, responsible for these extraordinary hallucinations in China and the Philippines.

item.title: Popular cannabis sleep gummies may have a hidden dark side
item.description: A cannabis-derived ingredient commonly found in sleep gummies may be more habit-forming than previously thought, with new research showing that repeated exposure caused tolerance and withdrawal symptoms in mice. Scientists warn that CBN may carry risks similar to THC, although its long-term effects in humans remain largely unknown.

item.title: Astronomers may have discovered the first moon beyond our Solar System
item.description: Astronomers have uncovered evidence of a bizarre, potentially historic discovery: the first moon ever detected beyond our Solar System. Unlike familiar moons, this mysterious object is at least as massive as Jupiter and orbits a brown dwarf, which itself circles a star. The unusual arrangement challenges traditional definitions of planets and moons, leaving scientists unsure what to call it.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden flaw that challenges 40 years of superconductor science
item.description: A superconducting material studied for 40 years has turned out to be far more complex than scientists believed. Advanced 3D imaging revealed a hidden patchwork of crystal structures, with unusually wide boundaries that may weaken superconductivity. The discovery challenges decades of scientific assumptions and could explain why some superconductors outperform others.

item.title: Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?
item.description: A small device that gently stimulates nerves through the ear could offer a new way to tackle stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial of 63 patients already taking medication, the treatment proved safe, easy to use at home, and well tolerated. Although it did not significantly outperform a placebo overall, patients with more severe hypertension showed promising reductions in blood pressure.

item.title: A hidden bias in human language challenges 70 years of science
item.description: A groundbreaking study challenges 70 years of assumptions about how human language works. By analyzing billions of word uses, scientists discovered that meaning is organized around power, danger, and order rather than emotion alone. Even more surprisingly, human language shows a powerful hidden preference for safety, suggesting that our words may reflect ancient survival instincts.

item.title: NASA’s asteroid Bennu samples reveal a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
item.description: Tiny samples from asteroid Bennu are rewriting scientists' understanding of how our Solar System formed. New evidence suggests that Bennu was born where material from the inner and outer Solar System mixed, with Jupiter playing a surprising role in shaping its formation.

item.title: Astronomers uncover a mysterious magnetic web above the Sun
item.description: The Sun’s seemingly peaceful regions are hiding a surprisingly complex magnetic world. Using a balloon-borne telescope high above Earth, scientists discovered delicate, thread-like magnetic structures woven through the solar atmosphere, apparently shaped by twisting motions on the Sun’s surface. They also mapped magnetic fields inside towering jets of solar material, revealing how those fields change with height.

item.title: Scientists propose a way to detect dangerous “mirror life” before it exists
item.description: Scientists have proposed a way to detect “mirror life,” a hypothetical form of life that could pose serious risks to humans, animals, and ecosystems if artificially created. Using special fluorescent molecules and a type of polarized light also used in 3D movie technology, researchers believe they could distinguish ordinary organisms from their mirror-image counterparts.
